... and then we can have some questions and I'll provide the
answers. So Chair, members of the committee, thank you for the opportunity to
appear before you today.
I'm speaking on behalf of the New Zealand Hemp Industries Association.
Firstly, I'd like to acknowledge the committee's continued interest in industrial
hemp.
We appreciate your engagement over the past two years and the opportunity to
continue the discussions following the recent regulatory reform.
The association also appreciates the work undertaken by the Ministry of Regulation.
The review represented the first significant reform of industrial hemp regulations
in 20 years. We publicly, excuse me, we publicly
welcome those changes. Today, I'd like to briefly discuss three things,
what has been achieved, what opportunities remain, and where government and
industry can work together over the next two years.
Industrial hemp is no longer a simple agricultural crop.
Around the world, it is becoming an important raw material for food, fiber,
construction materials, as you can see with the hemp block, and
internet, and textiles, bio composites, and the emerging
bioeconomy. New Zealand has genuine competitive
advantages. We already have world-class farming systems,
excellent traceability, a strong research sector, and an
international reputation for producing high-quality natural products.
The international market is growing rapidly.
Our opportunity is not simply to grow, it is to build high-value
processing industries and export both products and the
technologies developed here in New Zealand.
This is where the long-term economic value lies.
The recent reforms removed one of the industry's biggest frustrations.
Replacing the Ministry of Health license with a notification process has
significantly reduced compliant costs for growers
and those processing seed.
That was a practical and sensible decision, and increasing the
THC to 1% has given us access to more genetics.
Removing licenses has
also attracted considerable international attention because New Zealand has
demonstrated that industrial hemp can be regulated using a proportionate
risk-based approach. For that, the industry is genuinely
grateful.
However, these reforms primarily benefit cultivation, the growers, and the
seed processors. They did not substantially improve opportunities for full plant
utilization or manufacturing innovative products.
The largest barrier today sits further along the value chain.
Industrial hemp remains regulated under the Misuse of Drugs Act.
Oh.
Despite the United Nations Single Convention specifically excluding
low-THC industrial hemp grown for industrial and horticultural
purposes.
While growers can now produce the crop more easily, much of the plant cannot be
used commercially except through the situation medicinal
cannabis pathways.
That means that leaves and flowers and roots remain unavailable for health and
wellness products.
The current prohibition on hemp ingredients for production in companion animals
also limits commercial opportunities and reduces full plant
utilization.
These restrictions make investment more difficult.
Businesses are reluctant to invest in processing infrastructure where large
portions of the crop have no commercial pathway.
CBD is now the central issue. From an industry perspective, THC
is no longer the primary regulatory challenge, although getting out of
MODA remains the NZHIA's number one objective.
Modern industrial hemp contains extremely low levels of THC and routinely tests
well below regulatory thresholds.
The remaining challenge is CBD.
Because naturally occurring CBD is regulated as a prescription
medicine under the Medicines Act, industrial hemp biomass can generally
only enter the medicinal cannabis supply pathway.
Otherwise, we are forced to treat it as contaminant in our industrial hemp crops.
This effectively prevents development of a broader health and wellness
industry based on industrial hemp.
Addressing this issue would unlock significant innovation while maintaining
appropriate safeguards around therapeutic products.
Growing hemp is only the first step.
The real economic opportunity lies in processing, manufacturing, and developing
new products. That requires investment, it requires infrastructure, it
requires research, and it requires confidence that regulations
will continue evolving in a practical and evidence-based manner.
The association is encouraged by the strong relationships we have developed with
research organizations, universities, and innovation centers across New Zealand.
The capability exists. What is needed now is a regulatory environment that
allows investment to follow.
Looking ahead, the Ministry for Regulation has committed to reviewing these
regulations again in two years. That provides an excellent opportunity.
Between now and then, we can gather evidence, support responsible industry
growth,
and identify when further improvements can safely be made.
The NZHA is already contributing through education, industry guidance, and the
New Zealand
Hemp Industries Association Seed Product, helping new growers
adopt best practices while maintaining industry integrity.
Our requests, we respectfully ask the committee to continue
supporting practical and evidence-based reform.
In particular, we encourage government to continue progressing, getting
industrial hemp out of the Misuse of Drugs Act,
finally
allowing us to realize the full plant utilization and releasing us from the
burdens and regulations. Review the treatment of naturally
occurring CBD and low-THC industrial hemp that's leading to that health and
wellness industry. Support development of a health products framework.
Revisit the restrictions of hemp for companion and production animals
using evidence-based risk assessment.
Support research, standards, and processing capability that will allow New Zealand
to compete internationally and encourage investment into commercially viable
hemp businesses and regional processing infrastructure.
These are practical steps that will help industry grow responsibly while creating
regional jobs, supporting innovation, and contributing to New Zealand's emerging
bio-economy.
The 2026 reforms were an important milestone, and the industry
sincerely thanks the government and officials for the progress that has been made,
but they are only the beginning. We now have an opportunity to build a modern
industrial hemp industry that delivers economic, environmental, and regional
development benefits for New Zealand.
Our association looks forward to continuing to work constructively with government
and with this committee ahead of the next review.
Thank you,
and over to questions.
Thanks, Richard. We'll go straight to Mark Cameron, News.
Good morning, Richard, and thank you so much for
your time. We're very grateful for your time.
I'm interested to know,
obviously you'll have a pipeline of opportunity
costs and opportunities gained.
Where do you see yourself in five years' time?
We've
certainly seen this committee very, very active in trying to create an
environment that would give the hemp industry all the opportunities it

But you surely to goodness have a pipeline of aspiration, and what does that look

Well, if we're looking for a five-year horizon, then
one of the milestones will be the review of the Ministry for Regulation's-
Yeah
changes that they made this year. So that's in two years' time.
So we'll be working towards that to provide the information and evidence to
support the removal of low-THC industrial hemp out of the
Misuse of Drugs Act, because we're just another agricultural,
arable, or horticultural crop.
Mm.
And that would really free us up. So the regulations as they
stand did make a difference for the grower.
They no longer need a license. They can just notify the police and Ministry of
Primary Industries.
So that's the supply chain. But that's not really where the bottleneck sits.
It's the value chain is where we need to be developing innovative
products. So in five years' time, I'd like to see pet foods
available. Well, within one or two years, I would like to see pet foods available.
I'd like to see some trials done in the very short term on production
animals, because we only have a very small amount of these co-products
coming out of the hemp seed industry that could be used rather than being put into
a 40-foot container and shipped overseas-
Mm
... or disposed in a landfill. So, full plant
utilization means that we need the economics of all those parts
of the plant to work in our favor, and we need access to those markets.
So working through with MPI, ACVM on the
issue of production animals, which
was ruled out of scope from the Ministry
of Regulation's
deliberations, so they couldn't do anything with that particular issue.
Now, that was one of the biggest issues facing the industry.
So great, the growers are moving forward, but without those markets, it's very
burdensome still in the sense that we don't have access to the economics that we
need. So the animal food issue would be a great
one to overcome in the next five years.
And this treatment of CBD as a prescription medicine under the Medicines Act
complicates things unnecessary for industrial hemp.
The medicinal cannabis scheme has its own way of doing things.
They have their own regulatory
involvement with the Ministry of Health.
We are now no longer really involved with the Ministry of Health unless we want to
import or export because of that low level of THC.
But going back to the CBD, it's a massive problem because it's
naturally occurring in our plant, as are a number of other cannabinoids that all
have commercial interest, along with terpenes and flavonoids.
So
not being able to make products from the leaf and the
flower and the roots is a massive problem.
So our arable industry for food and fiber, that's going to continue to go
ahead, as we've discussed, without the need for a license.
That's removed again, a burdensome
regulation that cost money for compliance.
So that's gone. But
when we look at the horticultural industry, which is this part where we're looking
at these health and wellness products, it's really problematic because
there's global demand for them. There's Demand in New Zealand for them.
But we can't access that market because of the treatment of the Medicines
Act
making CBD a prescription medicine.

and significant money would be involved because you're leading to
export-led
market development. And that's where our aspirational
goals and

the biggest number in there for export potential was in that health and

as that's a global commodity, and that could get up there with the wine
industry, where we work together and keep the standards high for

This industry is one of probably the few industries currently that

So if that continues, which it will, then there's real economic

getting close to the aspirations of moving it way
beyond the $30 million mentioned in another report,
and growing from there.

Future growth, yeah

and bypass the New Zealand economy to the straight away,
go global from day one. So which is great for the global community, but not

in the gray area. We argued that the roots are part of the stem, so
